title: Why Do Leaves Change Color in Fall?
description: The reds and golds of fall were hiding inside the leaf all summer. A reading article about chlorophyll, shortening days, and trees getting ready for winter.

body.heading: A costume change with a secret
paragraphs: Every fall, green trees put on a show: red maples, golden birches, orange oaks. It looks as if the leaves are painted new colors for the season. The truth is stranger and better — most of those colors were inside the leaf all along, hidden under green.
To understand the reveal, you first need to meet the green itself.

body.heading: Stop and think
paragraphs: Leaves are a tree's kitchens — they cook food from sunlight. Before reading on, think: what might happen to a leaf's cooking if the days got shorter and colder, and sunlight grew scarce? Predict, then check your prediction.

body.heading: The green fades first
paragraphs: The green in a leaf is a chemical called chlorophyll — the part that catches sunlight for cooking food. All summer, the tree replaces chlorophyll as fast as it wears out, so leaves stay deep green. But as fall days shorten, the tree begins shutting down its kitchens for the winter. It stops replacing the chlorophyll.

The old chlorophyll fades — and as the green drains away, the yellows and oranges that were always in the leaf (from pigments called carotenoids, the same family that colors carrots) finally show through. They were never added. They were unmasked.

body.heading: Where red comes from
paragraphs: Reds and purples are a different story: many trees make those pigments fresh in the fall, in leaves that hold leftover sugars. Bright sunny days plus cold (but not freezing) nights produce the most brilliant reds — which is why some autumns are spectacular and others are a little dull, depending on the weather.

Soon after, the leaf's connection to the tree seals off completely, and the leaf lets go. It is not waste, exactly: fallen leaves rot into the soil and return their minerals to the tree's roots. Even in letting go, the leaf gives back.

body.heading: Words to know
paragraphs: Chlorophyll — the green chemical in leaves that catches sunlight for making food.
Pigment — any chemical that gives something its color.
Carotenoids — yellow and orange pigments hiding in leaves (and carrots) all year.
Deciduous — trees that drop all their leaves each fall, unlike evergreens.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Pennsylvania's fall colors are famous — people travel just to see them. Which tree near your home puts on the best show, and what colors does it choose?
2. Evergreen trees keep their needles all winter. What might be the advantage of keeping leaves — and the advantage of dropping them? Every strategy has a price; what does each tree pay?

takeaway: Fall colors are mostly an unmasking: as trees stop replacing green chlorophyll, hidden yellows and oranges show through — while reds are made fresh from leftover sugars on bright, cold days.
